paragraphs.heading: What builds a mountain
paragraphs.text: Mountains form through a variety of geological processes tied to large-scale movements of Earth's crust, the tectonic plates. Mountain building is called the orogenic process. Folding, faulting, volcanic activity, metamorphism and igneous intrusion can all be part of it. Mountains come in five main types: volcanic, fold, plateau, fault-block and dome. From the late 18th century, geosyncline theory was used to explain much mountain building, until plate tectonics replaced it in the 1960s.

paragraphs.heading: Volcanic mountains
paragraphs.text: Moving tectonic plates create volcanoes along plate boundaries, and those volcanoes erupt and form mountains. A volcanic arc system is a string of volcanoes close to a subduction zone, the place where a sinking oceanic plate's crust melts. Most volcanoes lie in a band that encircles the Pacific Ocean, called the Pacific Ring of Fire. A second band runs from the Mediterranean across Asia and joins the Pacific band in the Indonesian Archipelago.

paragraphs.heading: Shield and composite cones
paragraphs.text: The most important kinds of volcanic mountain are shield volcanoes and composite cones, also called stratovolcanoes. A shield volcano has a gently sloping cone because the material it emits, mainly basalt, has low viscosity. The classic example is Mauna Loa, whose slope is 4°-6°. A composite volcano rises more steeply, at 33°-40°, because its material has higher viscosity. Its eruptions are more violent and less frequent than those of shield volcanoes. Vesuvius, Kilimanjaro, Mount Fuji and Mount Rainier are examples.

paragraphs.heading: Fold mountains
paragraphs.text: When plates collide, or one rides over another in subduction, they tend to buckle and fold, and mountains form. Volcanic arcs form at boundaries between an oceanic plate and a continental one, while folding happens at boundaries between two continental plates. Most of the major continental ranges are associated with thrusting and folding. The Balkan Mountains, the Jura and the Zagros mountains are examples.

paragraphs.heading: Block mountains
paragraphs.text: A block mountain can result when a fault block is raised or tilted. The higher blocks are called horsts and the troughs are called grabens. When the surface spreads apart it causes tensional forces. If those forces are strong enough to split a plate, a center block drops down relative to the blocks on either side. The Sierra Nevada range is an example. It is a block 650 km long and 80 km wide, made of many portions tipped gently west, and its east-facing slips rise abruptly to give the highest mountain front in the continental United States.

paragraphs.heading: High margins without a model
paragraphs.text: Some passive continental margins are elevated. Examples are the Scandinavian Mountains, eastern Greenland, the Brazilian Highlands and Australia's Great Dividing Range. Unlike orogenic mountains, these have no widely accepted geophysical model to explain them. The different margins most likely share one mechanism of uplift, which may be related to far-field stresses in the lithosphere of Earth. On this view they can be likened to giant folds in the lithosphere, where the folding comes from horizontal compression acting on the zone in which thin crust passes to thick.

paragraphs.heading: Predicting the shapes
paragraphs.text: Several of the crustal movements that lead to mountains are associated with faults. These movements can be analysed to predict, for example, how high a raised block will be and how wide the rift between blocks will be. Early bent plate models that predicted fractures and fault movements have developed into today's kinematic and flexural models.
